pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Botrytis bunch rot is caused by the fungus Botrytis cinerea .

type_of_disease.quote: Botrytis bunch rot is caused by the fungus Botrytis cinerea .

value: Foliar
Stem
affected_parts.quote: Prior to fruit ripening, early-season shoot blight may occur following prolonged warm moist conditions caused by frequent spring rains. ... Infections often occur in leaf axils causing shoots to wilt or break off.

summary.value: Early-season shoot blight produces patches of soft brown tissue and death of infected plant parts, with infections in leaf axils causing shoots to wilt or break off. At veraison, individually infected berries turn brown on white cultivars or reddish in red and black cultivars, and epidermal cracks develop fungal growth with a characteristic gray, velvety appearance.
summary.quote: Patches of soft brown tissue develop resulting in the death of the infected plant part. Infections often occur in leaf axils causing shoots to wilt or break off. At veraison, individually infected berries in a cluster turn brown on white cultivars or reddish in red and black cultivars.

diagnostic_features.value: Epidermal cracks form in which fungal growth produces mycelium and spores, resulting in the characteristic gray, velvety appearance of infected berries; under high humidity infected berries become covered with a gray growth of fungus mycelium.
diagnostic_features.quote: epidermal cracks will form in which fungal growth produces mycelium and spores, resulting in the characteristic gray, velvety appearance of infected berries.

value: Noble rot
look_alikes.quote: both noble rot and gray mold symptoms are observed in sympatry, in the same vineyards, on the same plant, and sometimes within the same grapes

value: Promote good air circulation and light penetration by proper pruning, controlling weeds and suckers, and positioning or removing shoots for uniform leaf development.
Where possible, rows should be planted in the direction of the prevailing wind.
Removal of leaves around clusters (or basal leaves immediately after berry set) before bunch closing reduces losses caused by Botrytis.
Canopy management practices such as shoot thinning, hedging, and leaf removal can be used to manage canopy density when appropriate.
Design vineyards to the anticipated vigor of the site to produce balanced canopies with moderate shoot vigor that optimize leaf and cluster exposure.
Prevent wounding by controlling insects, birds, and other grape diseases; manage insect populations that produce entry wounds.
Avoid unnecessary irrigation or nitrogen fertilization that may promote excessive canopy growth.

Apply effective fungicides at appropriate times: between bloom and pea-size berries if the canopy interior remains dry, otherwise before rainfall at bloom or after veraison; treat late-harvest grapes prior to bunch closure and as needed before harvest.
Alternate fungicides with different modes of action within and between seasons to prevent fungicide resistance.
Use resistant cultivars when practical.
Organically acceptable methods: canopy/cultural management plus sprays of Organic JMS Stylet Oil and Serenade.

Conventional fungicide options include CYPRODINIL (Vangard WG), FENHEXAMID (Elevate 50WDG), PYRIMETHANIL (Scala SC), FLUOPYRAM + TEBUCONAZOLE (Luna Experience), CYPRODINIL + FLUDIOXONIL (Switch 62.5WG), DIFENOCONAZOLE + CYPRODINIL (Inspire Super), IPRODIONE (Rovral 4F), PYRACLOSTROBIN + BOSCALID (Pristine), NARROW RANGE OIL (JMS Stylet), BACILLUS SUBTILIS (Serenade Max), ISOFETAMID (Kenja 400SC).
treatments.quote: By employing cultural control methods, properly applying fungicides, and using resistant cultivars when practical, the disease can be managed.
